title: Manifest And Route: Delaunay Triangulations
notes: Open by grounding the lecture in the assigned source span and the chapter notebook. The through-line is not a catalogue of equivalent definitions; it is a conversion from terrain interpolation pressure into a computable planar graph. Preview the sequence: triangulations and flips, Voronoi duality, empty-circle tests, randomized insertion, point location, and the abstract configuration-space analysis.

title: Terrain Samples To A Polyhedral Surface
notes: Use the terrain story only long enough to motivate why a triangulation matters. Heights are known at sample points, so a triangulation chooses which triples define planar facets between samples. The geometric quality of those triangles changes the interpolated surface even when all measured heights are identical at the vertices.

title: A Bad Flip Can Manufacture A Bad Ridge
notes: Focus attention on one quadrilateral. Two diagonal choices interpolate the same four heights, but one diagonal may create long, skinny triangles whose planes connect distant samples across the feature. This is the informal reason the chapter ranks triangulations by angles before it ever names the Delaunay graph.

title: Triangulation Counts And Local Moves
notes: Now formalize the finite object. For n non-collinear points and k points on the convex-hull boundary, every triangulation has the same number of triangles and edges. That invariant makes local edge flips meaningful: flips move through a finite state space without changing the global count.

title: Angle Vector And Illegal Edge
notes: Introduce the angle vector as a lexicographic quality certificate. The illegal-edge definition is local: in a convex quadrilateral, the current diagonal is illegal when replacing it increases the sorted angle vector. Students should see that this is a local move designed to improve the global smallest-angle priority.

title: In-Circle Predicate
notes: The local angle test becomes practical through the in-circle predicate. For an oriented triangle, the sign of a lifted determinant tells whether the fourth point lies inside, on, or outside the circumcircle. The determinant visual is intentionally small; the main message is that legal-edge testing is a robust geometric predicate.

title: Legal Triangulation Terminates
notes: Describe the all-flips procedure as a proof device rather than as the efficient algorithm. Each illegal flip strictly improves the angle vector in a finite set of triangulations, so infinite cycling is impossible. When the process stops, every edge is legal, which will later match the Delaunay condition.

title: Voronoi Dual Becomes DG(P)
notes: Reconnect to Chapter 7. Join two sites when their Voronoi cells share an edge; the resulting straight-line graph is the Delaunay graph. The deck deliberately centers this duality instead of the lower convex hull, because dual Voronoi edges make the empty-circle and adjacency tests visually immediate.

title: Empty Circle Characterization
notes: Present the central certificate. Two sites form a Delaunay edge exactly when some empty circle has both sites on its boundary, and a Delaunay triangle has an empty circumcircle. This is the bridge between Voronoi vertices, legal edge tests, and the randomized construction.

title: Delaunay Optimizes Angles
notes: Tie the quality criterion back to Delaunay structure. Legal triangulations are Delaunay triangulations, and Delaunay triangulations maximize the angle vector among triangulations, up to degeneracies where several triangulations complete the same Delaunay graph. This explains why the data-independent rule improves terrain interpolation.

title: Randomized Incremental Setup
notes: Move from characterization to construction. The randomized algorithm shuffles the points, surrounds them with symbolic sentinel points, and inserts one point at a time into the current Delaunay triangulation. Only the region near the inserted point can change, so the global update becomes a set of local legalizations.

title: Insert Point: Triangle Case Versus Edge Case
notes: Separate the two geometric insertion cases. If the new point lies inside one triangle, replace that triangle by three. If it lies on an existing edge, remove the two adjacent triangles and replace them by four. The following legalization phase is identical in spirit: test the old boundary edges that may now be illegal.

title: LEGALIZE_EDGE Cascade
notes: Paraphrase the recursive procedure without copying pseudocode. When a boundary edge fails the in-circle test, flip it, then test the two newly exposed edges opposite the inserted point. The cascade is finite because each flip is a legalizing move, and it is local because only triangles incident to the changed region need attention.

title: Correctness: New Edges Are Delaunay
notes: Give the correctness proof as a certificate story. Edges from the inserted point to vertices of the containing triangle are supported by circles that can be tightened around the new point. After a flip, the new diagonal is also supported by an empty-circle witness. Therefore the algorithm never creates a fundamentally non-Delaunay new edge.

title: Point-Location DAG With Sentinels
notes: The algorithm still needs to find the triangle containing the next point. The history DAG records replaced triangles and points queries through the replacement children. Sentinels give a stable outer frame, so every real input point is inside the maintained triangulation and the search has a well-defined starting triangle.

title: Backwards Analysis Dashboard
notes: Summarize the expected-time lens. Look backward from a random stage: the last inserted point is equally likely among the r current points, and only features incident to that point disappear when it is removed. Since a planar Delaunay graph has linear complexity, the expected structural change per stage is constant.

title: Configuration Space And Consequences
notes: Close with the starred framework. A configuration space packages the objects that can appear, the small defining set that creates one, and the conflict set that destroys it. Delaunay corners fit this pattern, giving the cost bound for point location history and the final expected O(n log n) construction result.
